problems.stem: A designer describes a platform by listing: "quizzes, discussion forums, gradebook, badges." Why is this not yet an affordance analysis?
options: The list is too short; a real analysis names at least ten features.
It names features the tool has, not the learner actions those features make easy, hard, or impossible.
Badges should never appear in an instructional platform.
Affordance analysis requires screenshots, not text.
problems.explanation: An affordance is a relationship between the tool and a learner action. A feature list says what exists; an affordance analysis says what the learner can readily do.

problems.stem: The assigned LMS will not auto-grade open-response essays. A teammate proposes a paid plugin to force auto-grading. What is the stronger first move for the storyboard?
options: Buy the plugin immediately so the workflow stays fully automated.
Ask whether the no-auto-grade constraint actually protects a learning purpose, since essay feedback may require human judgment the design should keep.
Remove the essay task and replace it with a multiple-choice item.
Ignore the constraint and assume IT will solve it later.
problems.explanation: Not every constraint is a defect. A constraint that forces human review of essays may protect the learning goal, so interrogate it before engineering around it.

problems.stem: A storyboard frame calls for drag-to-rank branching with inline video annotation, but the delivery platform is a basic LMS page that only supports linked pages and embedded video. What does this reveal?
options: The platform is broken and should be replaced.
The design was authored for an imaginary platform; it must be revised to the affordances the real delivery tool can render.
Branching is never appropriate in instructional design.
Video annotation always degrades learning, so removing it is automatically correct.
problems.explanation: Designing for an idealized tool produces interactions the real platform cannot deliver. Anchor each interaction to the actual delivery affordances.

problems.stem: You must justify keeping a forum-based reflection even though the LMS forum threads collapse on mobile, where 60 percent of learners read. Which justification is defensible?
options: The forum looks better than alternatives on a desktop monitor.
Because 60 percent read on mobile, you redesign the reflection as a single-prompt journal that renders on mobile, accepting the forum's mobile constraint as decisive evidence.
Keep the forum and tell learners to switch to a laptop.
Remove reflection entirely to avoid the rendering issue.
problems.explanation: When a platform constraint (mobile thread collapse) collides with a learner reality (60 percent on mobile), the constraint becomes decisive evidence that should reshape the design.
